title: As hard to hold as the wind
hookLine: Arjuna says the mind is as hard to hold as the wind, and Krishna agrees
carry: the mind is held by practice and letting go
tomorrow: a leaf, a flower, a fruit and water

lines: AS HARD TO HOLD AS THE WIND.
cards: Plans made in a quiet week have a way of dissolving once the busy weeks come back. Arjuna knew the problem from the inside.
In chapter six of the Gita, Krishna has been describing a mind that rests even and steady, and Arjuna pushes back. The mind, he says, is restless, turbulent, strong and stubborn.
Holding it still seems to me as hard as holding the wind. It's a very human moment: that sounds lovely, but I don't think I can. And Krishna doesn't argue.

teach.b: His answer, in paraphrase: no doubt, the mind is restless and hard to hold. But it can be held by abhyasa and vairagya. Abhyasa is practice, the same thing done again and again.
Vairagya is letting go, loosening the grip of wanting. No secret technique. Just practice, and a looser hand.

teach.h: THIS WEEK: THE LEAF, ALL BEINGS, THE GIFT, THE GUEST.
teach.b: Look back over this week through that pair. We began with karma. In chapter five, the true renouncer neither hates nor craves, and the lotus leaf sits in the water all day without getting wet.
That's vairagya: staying in the work, letting the results roll off.

teach.h: A YEAR OF SERVICE IS A RHYTHM.
teach.b: Then we started designing a year of service. Delight in the good of all beings gave the reason. Svadharma gave the where: your own service, done imperfectly.
The gift gave four questions: why, what back, when, to whom. The guest gave the door. All of that is a design.
What it still needs is abhyasa. A year of service isn't one big decision. It's a rhythm: one day a week, one evening a month, one gift each season, one meal shared when the calendar comes round.
Abhyasa, on this reading, is more about returning than about intensity.

teach.h: A MISSED DAY IS WATER ON THE LEAF.
teach.b: And vairagya keeps the rhythm from turning into a tally of hits and misses, because the day you miss, or the gift that goes unthanked, is just water on the leaf. Arjuna said the mind was like the wind.
He said there's a way to hold it, and it looks a lot like showing up again.

how: Some Hindus keep service in a regular rhythm, such as a weekly shift in a temple kitchen or giving tied to festivals in the calendar, and teachers point to the Gita's pairing of abhyasa and vairagya, practice and letting go, for steadying the mind.

o: a strict rule never to miss a single day
practice, the same thing returned to again and again
one great effort, made once and then finished

s: Krishna tells Arjuna the mind is actually easy to hold
he agrees it's restless and hard to hold, then names practice and letting go.
Arjuna compares holding the mind to holding the wind
it's his own picture, in chapter six.
the Gita's answer to a restless mind is one secret technique
it's abhyasa and vairagya: practice and letting go.

games.q: you're Krishna. your student says the mind is as hard to hold as the wind. what do you say?
o: that's not true; it's easy once you try.
you're right, it's hard; it's held by practice and letting go.
then give up on stilling it.
games.why: Krishna agrees the mind is restless and hard to hold, and says it is held by abhyasa and vairagya.

practice: Let the breath be the practice, in, out, again, and when the mind runs off, as it will, notice where it went and come back without scolding: abhyasa and vairagya in miniature.
Then let this week's pieces come up one at a time, the leaf, the good of all beings, your own service, the gift, the guest, and ask of each one question, how often, letting a rhythm suggest itself.
If you pray, you can offer that rhythm to the one you pray to.

wordCard.voice: Abhyasa. Practice that repeats, held together with vairagya, a loose hand on the results.
